summary: This bill blocks the Secretary of Labor from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the OSHA proposed rule on heat injury and illness prevention in outdoor and indoor workplaces (89 Fed. Reg. 70698) or any substantially similar standard.

scores.thoughts: The bill does not authorize, appropriate, or alter any federal spending. It simply blocks OSHA from finalizing one specific workplace safety rule. No direct or indirect fiscal impact is described.
No provisions address taxes, tax rates, credits, or revenue measures of any kind.
The blocked OSHA rule concerns workplace heat safety rather than health insurance coverage, public programs, or market-based delivery of medical care.
The bill contains no language related to firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration pathways, border enforcement, visas, or related protections.
The legislation does not touch on reproductive health services or abortion access.
No references to defense spending, military policy, or national security appropriations appear in the text.

While heat-related illness can be exacerbated by climate trends, the bill targets an OSHA occupational safety standard rather than environmental regulations, EPA rules, or climate policy. The connection is too indirect to register a nonzero score.
The measure does not modify welfare programs, SNAP, unemployment insurance, or other safety-net entitlements.
No provisions relate to schools, federal education funding, school choice, or privatization.
The bill is silent on drug enforcement, decriminalization, or controlled-substance regulation.
Nothing in the text addresses sentencing, policing, rehabilitation, or criminal procedure.
No trade agreements, tariffs, or globalization measures are mentioned.
The bill neither authorizes new spending nor contains deficit-reduction mechanisms.
The legislation does not address legal protections or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No foreign assistance, international aid, or State Department programs are implicated.
The bill contains no election administration, voting access, or voter-ID provisions.
No technology regulation, data privacy, or platform oversight language is present.

The bill directly prohibits OSHA from implementing a workplace heat-injury prevention standard. This removes a regulatory requirement that would have imposed new obligations on employers to protect workers from heat illness. By blocking the rule, the legislation favors employer flexibility over additional mandated worker protections, aligning with the positive end of the scale.
The text does not engage with religious exemptions, civil-rights enforcement, or anti-discrimination rules.
